purpose: Elacestrant is used to treat a certain type of breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause and in men. It is specifically for hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer that has spread or gotten worse after other treatments. Your doctor may prescribe it if your cancer has a specific gene change called an ESR1 mutation.
how_it_works: Breast cancer cells sometimes use the hormone estrogen to grow and spread. Elacestrant works by attaching to the estrogen receptor on cancer cells and then breaking it down, so estrogen can no longer fuel the cancer's growth. Think of it like removing the key that estrogen uses to start the engine of cancer cell growth.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, tiredness, vomiting, increased cholesterol levels, decreased appetite, diarrhea, low sodium levels in the blood, stomach pain, constipation, and hot flashes. Some people may also notice joint or muscle pain.
warnings: Elacestrant can cause harm to an unborn baby, so it is very important to use reliable birth control during treatment and for one week after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. It may also raise your cholesterol and other fats in your blood, so your doctor will monitor these levels. Let your doctor know about all other medications you take, as some drugs can affect how well elacestrant works.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 345 mg taken by mouth once a day with food. Taking it with food helps reduce nausea. Try to take it at the same time each day, and swallow the tablets whole. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day, but skip it if it is almost time for your next dose — never double up.
